Every changed golden is a pure function of the blob bytes: the delta is the blob substring plus recomputed offsets/lengths derived from it. Intentional spec change, corroborated by independent oracles: (1) the BSV Spend interpreter e2e suite (packages/runar-testing oppushtx-binding.test.ts) verifies the new blob ACCEPTS the genuine tx sighash preimage and REJECTS forged/decoupled and zeroed preimages (the BUG-100 exploit), across a 60-context sighash sweep plus 4 ground DER/low-S edge contexts (both malleation branches, 31-byte and 30-byte s); (2) the derived-key math (pubkey 02b405d7... = (2^248*Gx^-1 mod n)*G) was re-derived off-chain from the curve parameters alone; (3) all seven independently written tiers (TS, Go, Rust, Python, Ruby, Java, Zig) regenerate byte-identical goldens — conformance 72/72, sdk-output 59 cases x 7 SDKs clean, sdk-vertical 39/39 x 7 tiers, analyzer 24 pass / 0 fail; (4) 269 Go integration tests and 229 TS integration tests pass against a live bitcoin-sv regtest node, spending real covenant outputs that carry the new blob.

R-052 / CL-BUG-095 (no length validation on any Point argument in any tier; ecEncodeCompressed took the parity bit from the blob last byte) and R-053 / CL-BUG-096 (ecAdd(P, O) returned an off-curve blob while the always-on EC optimizer rewrote the same expression as the identity). The analyzer consumes conformance/tests/ec-demo/expected-script.hex verbatim and no analyzer logic changed, so this report moves as a pure function of the fixture hex. Re-measured, not assumed: re-analysing the OLD hex reproduces the committed report exactly. WIDENED from 4 vectors to 34, regenerated by tests/generate-vectors/bn254 against gnark-crypto. BN254/Groth16 ships Stack-IR codegen in the Go tier only, so cross-tier parity is definitionally vacuous for it and this file is the entire oracle for the pairing — the most security-critical operation in the Groth16 path. INDEPENDENT CHECK, and this file’s first consumer: conformance/scripts/check-bn254-pairing-invariants.mjs enforces bilinearity, degeneracy, non-degeneracy, field-element canonicity (< p) and a coverage floor over the checked-in bytes; run 2026-08-17 on this exact content, all invariants hold, and its own --self-test shows all 8 scenarios rejecting/passing as expected. REPRODUCIBILITY: tests/generate-vectors/verify-reproducible.sh re-runs every generator and diffs; on this tree all 22 vector files reproduce byte-for-byte, so the pinned bytes are what gnark-crypto and Plonky3 actually emit rather than a recorded claim.

Codegen change for #137 (the on-chain SLH-DSA verifier was FIPS-205 NON-CONFORMANT). Two verify-path deviations were fixed in the shared SLH-DSA emitter across all 7 tiers, and NEITHER ALONE was sufficient to accept the standard vector: (1) FIPS 205 Sec 11.2.1 -- H_msg's MGF1 seed must be R || PK.seed || SHA-256(R || PK.seed || PK.root || M); the emitter omitted the R || PK.seed prefix, which NIST added to mitigate multi-target long-message second-preimage attacks. (2) FIPS 205 Alg. 8 lines 8-11 -- wots_pkFromSig must restore the key pair address after setTypeAndClear(WOTS_PK) zeroes ADRS bytes 20-31; the emitter pushed four zero bytes and never restored the real leaf index. Evidence is an OFFICIAL KAT, not a self-golden: NIST ACVP SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s (internal) sigVer vector, tgId 31 / tcId 422, testPassed=true, vendored verbatim at conformance/runtime-vectors/slh-dsa-acvp-kat.json. The previous goldens were graded only against signatures this repo produced with the same buggy signer -- the BUG-101 self-consistency trap. Scripts shrank slightly (the PICKed key-pair address is cheaper than a 4-byte push); expected-ir.json did not move, because the change is confined to stack lowering. All 7 tiers emit byte-identical hex for this fixture (conformance 72/72 in both fold modes). This fixture is SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s (n=16, SHA-256-only per FIPS 205 Table 2) -- the EXACT parameter set the ACVP vector covers -- and it is verified END-TO-END THROUGH THE COMPILED SCRIPT, not merely through the off-chain helper, by packages/runar-testing/src/__tests__/post-quantum-slh-acvp-onchain.test.ts, which replays the NIST signature on @bsv/sdk's Spend interpreter and requires accept, plus reject on a 1-bit tamper. Both fixes were RED-proved: reverting either one individually turns that on-chain accept test red. Native Go verify is separately gated by TestOfficialKAT_SLHDSA_ACVP (packages/runar-go/crypto_kat_test.go), now an enforcing assertion rather than the xfail it replaced.

(2) FIPS 205 Alg. 8 lines 8-11 -- wots_pkFromSig must restore the key pair address after setTypeAndClear(WOTS_PK) zeroes ADRS bytes 20-31; the emitter pushed four zero bytes and never restored the real leaf index. Evidence is an OFFICIAL KAT, not a self-golden: NIST ACVP SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s (internal) sigVer vector, tgId 31 / tcId 422, testPassed=true, vendored verbatim at conformance/runtime-vectors/slh-dsa-acvp-kat.json. The previous goldens were graded only against signatures this repo produced with the same buggy signer -- the BUG-101 self-consistency trap. Scripts shrank slightly (the PICKed key-pair address is cheaper than a 4-byte push); expected-ir.json did not move, because the change is confined to stack lowering. All 7 tiers emit byte-identical hex for this fixture (conformance 72/72 in both fold modes). This fixture is SLH-DSA-SHA2-256f. The vendored ACVP file carries no vector for this parameter set, so it is NOT directly KAT-verified; it is the SAME emitter code path, parameterised by (n, h, d, a, k), whose 128s instantiation IS NIST-verified end-to-end through the compiled script (see the post-quantum-slhdsa entry). CAVEAT, neither introduced nor closed by this fix and tracked separately: FIPS 205 Sec 11.2.2/11.2.3 mandate SHA-512 (and 128-byte padding) for the 192/256 parameter sets' H_msg/PRF/H/T, and Bitcoin Script has no OP_SHA512, so 192s/192f/256s/256f remain non-conformant on that axis and are self-consistent only. Only the 128-bit parameter sets are FIPS-205 conformant on-chain.

NEW-014: `&&` / `||` now SHORT-CIRCUIT on-chain. They lowered to OP_BOOLAND / OP_BOOLOR, which are binary stack ops -- both operands must already be ON the stack, so both were evaluated unconditionally. spec/semantics.md 3.7 licensed that with "This is safe in Runar because all expressions are pure (no side effects beyond assert)", but purity is not TOTALITY: 10 of the same document lists division by zero as a runtime failure, and OP_SPLIT / OP_NUM2BIN abort out of range. Evaluating the operand the source skipped therefore ABORTED the script, so the ordinary defensive guard `assert(d === 0n || (100n / d) > 1n)` compiled to a locking script the chain rejects for exactly the input the guard exists to protect -- a permanently unspendable UTXO -- while the AST interpreter (which short-circuits) reported success. `&&` / `||` now desugar to the ternary, which stack lowering already emits as real OP_IF / OP_ELSE control flow (3.9 already specified the untaken arm as unevaluated), so the moved bytes are OP_BOOLAND/OP_BOOLOR (0x9a/0x9b) becoming OP_IF/OP_ELSE/OP_ENDIF (0x63/0x67/0x68). EVIDENCE IS THE DIFFERENTIAL ORACLE, NOT A SELF-GOLDEN: the OLD bytes are REJECTED by @bsv/sdk's real Spend.validate() on inputs the source accepts. The three specific consensus rejections pinned in packages/runar-testing/src/__tests__/shortcircuit-consensus-vm.test.ts are "OP_DIV cannot divide by zero!" (d=0 through a `||` zero-guard), "OP_SPLIT requires the first stack item to be a non-negative number less than or equal to the size of the second-from-top stack item" (a guarded out-of-range substr), and "OP_NUM2BIN requires that the size expressed in the top stack item is large enough to hold the value expressed in the second-from-top stack item" (a guarded undersized num2bin). That suite pins BOTH directions for every short-circuiting case -- the input that must not reach the right operand, the input that must reach it and hold, and the input that must reach it and reject -- so a compiler that simply dropped the right operand could not pass it. All 7 tiers emit byte-identical hex and IR for this fixture in both fold modes (conformance 72/72), and the regeneration moved ONLY the six files of the three fixtures whose sources use `&&` / `||`; a control regeneration on the unpatched tree was a byte-for-byte no-op, so every moved byte is attributable to this change alone. THIS FILE: the ANF IR (the desugar happens in ANF lowering, so the IR moves too) for fixture `bitwise-ops`, whose source examples/ts/bitwise-ops/BitwiseOps.runar.ts uses six `||` guards. Its bytes move because those operators change lowering; no other behaviour of the fixture changed.

First deploy-locking golden for the integer-boundary fixture (#162): the compiled 60-byte codePart with its single bigint constructor slot spliced, giving 138 bytes. The constructor value is 85070591730234615893513767959916445698 -- the 126-bit sum the contract asserts -- and it is the point of the case. Every other bigint slot in the sdk-output suite fits a machine word, so before this nothing in it spliced a constructor value wider than 8 bytes, and an SDK whose slot encoder narrowed to i64 would have produced a wrong locking script with nothing to catch it. That narrowing is precisely the compiler-side defect this PR fixes in the Zig tier, so the SDK side is now pinned against the same class of bug. The cross-check is not self-report: seven independently written deployment SDKs (TypeScript, Go, Rust, Python, Zig, Ruby, Java) each build the locking script from the artifact and are compared byte-for-byte against this pin AND against each other by the required 'SDK Output Conformance' job; a divergence in any single tier fails it. Verified locally at this hash: 60 sdk-output fixtures, coverage audit OK, integer-boundary PASS across all seven SDKs. The underlying compiled bytes are separately justified by the fixture's own goldenHashes entry in conformance/witnesses/integer-boundary.json, whose differential oracle executes an accept and a near-miss reject through a second engine.

NEW-004 fund-loss fix: the compiled bytes grew 27 -> 31 by four OP_BIN2NUM (0x81), one per numeric READ of a shift result (two shifts x two reads each). The old bytes are not merely different, they are REJECTED BY THE REAL CONSENSUS ENGINE: OP_LSHIFT/OP_RSHIFT preserve the operand's byte width, so `this.a << 3n` with a 1-byte `a` leaves a non-minimal buffer ([0x00], or [0x80] when the result lands on the sign bit), and the following OP_GREATERTHANOREQUAL reads it with requireMinimal and aborts with "non-minimally encoded script number" -- the contract deploys and its UTXO can never be spent. Measured, not argued: runTriModalExecution over this shape reported interpreter=accept, ScriptVM=accept, Spend.validate()=REJECT in both fold modes, because ScriptVM runs the upstream engine relaxed and only Spend.validate() applies the consensus rule set. The new bytes turn all 15 RED cases in packages/runar-testing/src/__tests__/bitwise-minimality-consensus.test.ts green against Spend.validate() while the 3 width-fitting controls and the 3 PR #141 chained-shift pins (2026-07-14-chained-shift-{and,or}-*, 2026-07-12-shift-truncation) stay green -- normalisation is at the numeric CONSUMER, so byte-array operand widths are untouched. Byte-identical across all 7 tiers in both fold modes; expected-ir.json did NOT move (the repair is in stack lowering, the ANF is unchanged).

NEW-004 fund-loss fix, same repair as conformance/tests/shift-ops: 96 -> 108 bytes, twelve OP_BIN2NUM (0x81), one per numeric READ of a byte-array result -- six producing ops (<<, >>, &, |, ^, ~) read twice each by `assert(x >= 0n || x < 0n)`. OP_AND, OP_XOR and OP_INVERT carry the identical defect to the shifts and were confirmed the same way: `q & 4n` with q=3 gives [0x00] and `~q` with q=127 gives [0x80], and runTriModalExecution reported interpreter=accept, ScriptVM=accept, Spend.validate()=REJECT ("non-minimally encoded script number") for both, i.e. deployed and unspendable. OP_OR cannot make a minimal PAIR non-minimal, but it propagates non-minimality from its operands -- `(q<<10) | (q<<11)` is [0x00]|[0x00] -- so it is normalised on the same footing; that is the only one of the twelve bytes that is defensive rather than load-bearing. Same evidence, same test file, same 7-tier byte-identical result in both fold modes; expected-ir.json did not move.

R-052 / CL-BUG-095 (no length validation on any Point argument in any tier; ecEncodeCompressed took the parity bit from the blob last byte) and R-053 / CL-BUG-096 (ecAdd(P, O) returned an off-curve blob while the always-on EC optimizer rewrote the same expression as the identity). Both defects were REPRODUCED before the fix by executing the emitted script on @bsv/sdk Spend with real secp256k1, not inferred from the bytes: ecOnCurve(G||0xff) returned TRUE, ecPointX on a 32-byte blob succeeded, ecEncodeCompressed(G||0x01) flipped the compressed sign from 02 to 03, and ecAdd(G, allZero64) returned cf88213f...169139c6 with ecOnCurve(result) false. This is the deployed locking script for the same contract, so it moves with the code part. The sdk-output suite compares all seven SDKs against this one golden, so the bytes are agreed by seven independent implementations rather than produced by one. Independent evidence for the NEW bytes, none of it self-graded: (1) packages/runar-testing r052-point-length-gate.test.ts and r053-ec-add-infinity.test.ts execute every claim on the real Spend interpreter, and each guard was falsified in turn (neutering it reddens exactly the matching assertions and nothing else); (2) the pre-existing independent-oracle suites still pass unchanged against the new codegen - ec-crossverify / ec-mul-k2 / ec-mul-scalars grade against @bsv/sdk secp256k1, ec-degenerate-add and ec-on-curve-canonicity grade against OpenSSL via node:crypto ECDH, and p256-p384-ecdsa-verify grades against RFC 6979 vectors; (3) all seven independently written compilers regenerate these exact bytes byte-for-byte, each verified against the TS reference before any golden was touched; (4) an exhaustive sweep of all 78 conformance fixtures shows exactly 10 move and 68 are byte-unchanged, so the change is confined to the EC / P-256 / P-384 families.
